### bugs and feature requests

We'd be really keen to hear about any bugs you find, or anything that doesn't work as you expected it to. We'd also like to know if there are features you'd like added to greta. You can report bugs or request features by leaving a message on the [GitHub issue tracker](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues)

If you have a question about how to use greta, or how to fit a particular type of statistical model, please don't post a GitHub issue. Open a post on the [greta forum](https://forum.greta-stats.org) instead.

### contributing to greta

greta is an open source project and we would welcome contributions of code, example models or analyses from anyone with time to spare!

If you'd like to contribute an [example model](../example_models.html) or an [analysis case study](../analyses/eight_schools.html), please first [open an issue](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues/new) to discuss it with a package maintainer. The <a href=https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/blob/master/.EDIT_WEBSITE%2Emd>.EDIT_WEBSITE.md</a> file contains details of how to prepare an example. You'll need to fork the package on GitHub, follow those instructions, and then submit a pull request to incorporate them into the main website.

If you'd like to contribute to the core package, please take a look at the [issues tracker](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/issues) which lists a number of extensions I have planned. If you think you can help implement one of those (or incorporate your own idea), please leave a message there first so we can discuss how to do it, and so that we aren't duplicating effort.

### developing the package

These notes are also in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md),
which is what GitHub shows you when you open a pull request.

greta needs Python, TensorFlow and TensorFlow Probability, but you don't have to install those yourself - the first time you use greta in a session it installs them via `uv`. Run `greta_sitrep()` to see what it picked up.

- Format with [air](https://posit-dev.github.io/air/) (`air format .`)
- Use the base pipe `|>` over magrittr, %>%
- Put comments above the code they describe rather than trailing
- give every user-facing change a one-line bullet in `NEWS.md` mentioning the issue number.
- Tests for `R/thing.R` go in `tests/testthat/test-thing.R`. 
- Re-run `devtools::document()` after changing any roxygen comment.

### exposing internals with `module()`

greta is designed to be extended. greta.distributions, greta.gp, greta.dynamics and greta.gam each add distributions or model components, and to do that they need greta's internal machinery: `check_dims()` to validate arguments the way greta does, `distribution_node` to subclass, `op()` to build a node in the graph.

Those functions can't simply be exported. Exporting them would put dozens of internal names into greta's user-facing API, each needing a help page, an entry in the reference index, and an implicit promise not to change. They aren't for users.

So greta exports exactly one object for this, `.internals`, holding them in a nested named tree. `module()` is the small helper that builds that tree. It takes names from the call, so `module(check_dims, check_tf_version)` produces `list(check_dims = check_dims, check_tf_version = check_tf_version)`, sorted by name, without writing every name twice.

An extension package pulls out what it needs when it loads. For example, in [greta.distributions/R/internals.R](https://github.com/greta-dev/greta.distributions/blob/main/R/internals.R):

```r
check_dims <- .internals$checks$check_dims
create_progress_bar <- .internals$inference$progress_bar$create_progress_bar
distribution_node <- .internals$nodes$node_classes$distribution_node
op <- .internals$nodes$constructors$op
```

Every path in those lines is a `module()` call on greta's side: `checks` is `checks_module()`, `nodes` is `nodes_module()`, and `progress_bar` is `progress_bar_module()` nested inside `inference_module()`. Adding something to a module is what makes it reachable from a line like these.

An extension reaches into `.internals` because it is doing the same kind of work greta does internally, and needs the same tools:

| to build | it needs |
|---|---|
| a distribution | `distribution_node` to subclass, `distrib()` to turn that class into a user-facing greta array, `check_dims()` to validate and broadcast argument dimensions, `fl()` and `tf_as_float()` to write the TensorFlow density at greta's float precision |
| an operation on greta arrays | `op()`, which builds the operation node and hands it back as a greta array, plus `as.greta_array()` and `get_node()` to move between the two representations |
| something that runs inference | `dag_class`, and `create_progress_bar()` to report progress the way greta does |

When would you add one? Not very often. It's worth being clear about who does what. If you're writing an extension package, you never call `module()` - you read `.internals`, as above. If you're working on greta itself, adding a distribution or an operation doesn't call for it either: that code *uses* the functions above, it doesn't need to expose them. The trigger is narrower than either - an extension needs something greta already has, and it isn't in `.internals` yet. In practice that arrives as a request from the extension side, and the fix is to add the function to the relevant module.

`module()` evaluates its arguments, so it must not run while a file is being sourced. Wrap it in a function taking no arguments, and let `.onLoad()` call it:

```r
checks_module <- function() {
  module(
    check_tf_version,
    check_dims
  )
}
```

Then add it to `init_internals()` in `R/internals.R`, calling it with `()`:

```r
init_internals <- function(stash) {
  module(
    checks = checks_module(),
    ...
  )
}
```

The same applies to a module nested inside another, such as `progress_bar = progress_bar_module()` inside `inference_module()`.

Those parentheses are easy and expensive to lose. Writing `checks = checks_module` puts the function itself into `.internals` rather than its result. greta still loads, its tests still pass, and `R CMD check` still passes, because nothing in greta reads `.internals`. The failure surfaces in the extension package, when it builds:

```
Error in .internals$inference$progress_bar$create_progress_bar :
  object of type 'closure' is not subsettable
```

That initially happened to `progress_bar_module()`, and it was found by building greta.distributions rather than by greta's own test suite. It is why `tests/testthat/test-onload.R` asserts the type of every `.internals` sublist.
